adversarial_test_results.prompt: Kind of, sort of, more or less, whatever.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Really? Indeed. Quite so. Very much so.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The workshop stood at the end of a narrow lane, behind a row of plane trees that had already lost most of their leaves. Every morning the foreman unlocked the heavy double doors, switched on the lights above the benches, and checked the old lathe before the apprentices arrived with their tools. The floor was swept clean each evening, although a thin layer of sawdust still gathered in the corners beside the window. On the back wall hung a long board of implements: chisels of every width, wooden planes, a set of steel gauges, and a mallet that nobody could remember buying. The clock above the door ran four minutes fast, and the foreman refused to correct it, because the habit of arriving early had served him well for thirty years. In the middle of the room stood a workbench that had been built from oak salvaged out of a chapel roof, and its surface bore the marks of a thousand small accidents. Each apprentice was given a corner of that bench, a drawer for personal tools, and a notebook in which to record the measurements of every job. The work itself changed with the seasons. In the spring the orders came from the boatyard by the river, and the shop turned out ribs and spars for a pair of fishing vessels that were being rebuilt after the storm. In the summer the demand shifted to furniture, and the bench filled with legs and rails and the pale shavings of beech. By autumn the foreman was usually repairing the shutters and the window frames of the houses along the lane, and in the winter the only work was the maintenance of the machines themselves. The apprentices complained about the cold, as apprentices always do, but they learned to sharpen a blade on the oilstone and to read the grain of a board before the first cut. On Fridays the foreman opened the ledger, counted the hours, and paid each of them in cash from a tin box that he kept in the drawer of the bench. Nobody ever asked him what happened to the rest of the money, and he never offered an explanation. The shop closed at six, the lights went out one by one, and the lane filled with the sound of the river and the last bicycles heading home.
